transcript.answer: Otto uses one server-side key because OLT's TMS API gives it no other option. The delivered TMS External API authenticates with a single global `x-api-key` header. It has no user login, no login endpoint and no per-user credential. ADR-001 considered three options. Option A had each portal user present their own TMS credential for Otto to forward. It was rejected because that credential does not exist, so a customer cannot present it. Option B was also removed: re:cinq cannot exchange or hold a per-user credential that does not exist. (The excerpt I retrieved gives the rejection reason for A but not B. The spec states B's reason.) Option C was accepted: Otto holds one global `TMS_API_KEY` and enforces the customer boundary in its own code. OLT's non-negotiable requirement is that customers can only see their own bookings. Because the TMS cannot tell customers apart, Otto derives the customer number server-side from the authenticated identity and never takes it as a model-supplied tool input. `apps/api/src/tools/toolAuth.ts` re-verifies the token on every call. Each TMS tool also runs an `ownership` check. The ADR's assumption that the TMS does not scope responses per key is still pending confirmation from OLT (OC-1).

judgements.reason: The answer covers the single global TMS_API_KEY, the customer boundary enforced in Otto's code, and the TMS having no user-level auth, but it omits that per-user credentials are moot because the TMS issues one key per integration partner.

The answer says Otto holds one global TMS_API_KEY and enforces the customer boundary in its own code, and that forwarding is impossible because the TMS has no user-level auth; its point that the TMS uses only a single global key with no per-user credential covers the gold's 'one key per integration partner' rationale, and nothing contradicts the gold.
